role: Tax, with Omar on structure and governance
title: The Exit Is Taxed the Way You Built the Entry
summary: Selling a building and selling the company that owns it are two different transactions with two different tax results. The seller usually prefers to sell shares; the buyer usually prefers to buy the asset. Which one is even possible at exit is decided years earlier, when you choose how to hold the property.
body:
You do not choose your exit tax at the exit. You choose it on the day you decide how to hold the building. By the time a buyer arrives, the form of sale, and much of its tax, is already fixed.

Recall

Q. What are the three gates cross-border money must pass?

A. Registration with the state where required, permission to convert and remit under exchange rules or in practice, and a bank willing to carry the money under its know-your-customer duties.

Q. When a business is sold as a going concern, why can the value-added tax treatment differ from a sale of individual assets?

A. Because many value-added tax systems give special treatment to the transfer of a whole operating business, so that tax is not charged on the transfer itself. The conditions are strict and vary by country, so they must be checked before the sale is structured.

Q. What does "central management and control" mean in residence?

A. A test, used for companies and trusts in some countries, that places residence where the real high-level decisions are actually made, regardless of where the entity is registered.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer builds wealth at the exit. Every year of design, financing and construction converts into money on one day: the day of sale or refinance. If that day is badly structured, a large part of the gain can go to tax that a different structure, chosen earlier, would have deferred, reduced or shifted to a buyer who would have paid for the privilege. This week is about that day, and about the earlier days that decide it.

Omar sits with me because the tax answer depends entirely on the structure. You cannot fix the exit with a clever clause in the sale agreement. You fix it with the holding structure, chosen when the land was bought.

Two ways to sell the same building

In plain English: you can sell the building, or you can sell the box the building is in.

The professional framing is the choice between an asset sale, in which the owning company sells the property itself to the buyer, and a share sale, in which the shareholders sell the shares of the owning company, so the company, and the building inside it, change hands without the building being transferred at all. The building is the same. The legal event is different, and so is the tax.

In an asset sale, the company realises the gain on the property, usually pays tax on it at company level, and then the shareholders face a second layer of tax when the proceeds are paid out to them. The buyer takes the building at the price it paid, which becomes its new tax cost, so it can depreciate the building afresh. In a share sale, the shareholders realise a gain on their shares, usually once, and the company keeps its old tax cost in the building. The buyer inherits the company's history, including the latent gain inside it, and any old liabilities.

Why buyers and sellers want opposite things

Here is the tension. The seller usually prefers a share sale, because it can avoid tax at company level and may avoid transfer taxes on the land. The buyer usually prefers an asset sale, because it gets a fresh, higher tax cost and leaves old liabilities behind. Every exit negotiation is partly a negotiation about who bears this difference. Whether a share sale is even taxed differently from an asset sale depends on the country, on treaties, and on rules that look through property-rich shares; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers and an assumed tax rate for teaching only. A company owns a building with a tax cost of 6,000,000 dollars. A buyer offers 10,000,000 dollars. In an asset sale, the company has a gain of 4,000,000 dollars. At an assumed company tax rate of 25 percent, it pays 1,000,000 dollars, leaving 9,000,000 dollars to distribute, before any shareholder-level tax. In a share sale at a price reflecting the same building, the shareholders sell shares, and the company's 4,000,000 dollar latent gain stays inside the company, now owned by the buyer. A careful buyer will cut its price to reflect the tax it inherits. So the question is never only "which form is taxed less?" It is "how much will the buyer discount the price for the latent tax, and is that less than the tax I save?"

Say that out loud now.

An asset sale sells the building; a share sale sells the box. The buyer prices the latent tax in the box, so I compare the discount with the tax I save.

Recapture: the gain hiding inside depreciation

In plain English: if tax law let you deduct the building's wear and tear, and you then sell it for more than its written-down value, some of those deductions may be taken back.

The professional framing is recapture: on the sale of depreciable property, deductions previously claimed for depreciation, to the extent the sale price exceeds the depreciated tax cost, are brought back into income. Depending on the country, recapture may be taxed as ordinary income rather than as a capital gain, often at a higher effective rate [unverified — confirm independently].

A second worked example, hypothetical. A company bought a building for 8,000,000 dollars, of which 6,000,000 dollars was depreciable structure, and has claimed 1,500,000 dollars of depreciation, so the building's tax cost is now 6,500,000 dollars. It sells for 10,000,000 dollars. The 1,500,000 dollars of deductions is recaptured as income. The remaining 2,000,000 dollars above the original cost is a capital gain. Two pieces of the same profit, possibly taxed two different ways. In an asset sale the company faces this directly. In a share sale the recapture stays latent inside the company, and the buyer will want paying for it.

How the best do it

Institutional owners commonly hold each significant building in its own company, a single-purpose vehicle, partly for lender requirements and partly to keep exit choices open: a single-asset company can be sold as shares cleanly, without carrying other buildings or old liabilities. They also keep a tax file for each building from day one, recording tax cost, depreciation claimed and any elections, so that a buyer's diligence finds a clean history. A small developer can copy both: one building per company, and one tax-history file per building, started at acquisition.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: asset versus share decides who pays the company-level tax and recapture, and whether transfer taxes apply. Liability: a share buyer inherits the company's past, so it will demand indemnities from you. Banking: a sale usually triggers loan repayment or a lender's consent to the change of control. Governance: the board and shareholders must approve the sale in the form the documents require. Estate: how you hold the shares decides what your estate holds if you die before the sale. Exit: the choice between selling the building and selling the box must still be open when the buyer arrives.

Professional sign-off required: a tax adviser in each relevant country; a corporate lawyer on the sale agreement.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is holding a building in a way that leaves only one form of sale, or none that a buyer will accept, so the exit's tax is decided by default. The control is to decide, at acquisition, how the asset should be sold, and to choose the holding structure that keeps that option open.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner celebrates the headline price, then learns at closing that a buyer insisting on an asset sale has just added a layer of company tax and recapture he never modelled.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage taught that after-tax leakage separates the IRR you quote from the IRR investors keep. The exit is where most of that leakage is decided, and it is decided by a structure choice made in Week 55's sequencing step, years before anyone signs a sale agreement.

Recap

An asset sale sells the building; a share sale sells the company that owns it. Sellers usually prefer shares, buyers usually prefer assets, and the buyer prices any latent tax it inherits. Recapture brings back past depreciation as income. Decide the exit form at entry, and hold the building to keep that choice open.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: a composite exit priced as a share sale and taxed as an asset sale.
checklist: I decided at acquisition how this building should be sold at exit.
Each significant building sits in its own company.
I keep a tax-history file per building from day one.
I know the building's tax cost and the depreciation claimed to date.
I can estimate the latent tax inside the company today.
I compare a buyer's price discount with the tax a share sale saves.
I know whether the loan allows a change of control.
My will and estate plan reflect how I hold the shares.
head: Field checklist
speak: At exit I can sell the building or sell the company that owns it. In an asset sale the company sells the property, usually pays tax on the gain at company level, including recapture of past depreciation, and then shareholders may be taxed again when the cash is paid out. The buyer gets a fresh, higher tax cost. In a share sale the shareholders sell the shares, the building stays inside the company with its old tax cost, and the buyer inherits the latent gain and any old liabilities. Sellers usually prefer shares; buyers usually prefer assets, and a careful buyer cuts its price for the latent tax it takes on. So the real question is whether the discount is smaller than the tax I save. That choice is decided at entry: one building per company, a tax-history file from day one, and an exit form chosen when the land is bought.
terms: Asset sale — a sale in which the owning company sells the property itself, realising any gain at company level.
Share sale — a sale of the shares of the owning company, so the property changes hands without itself being transferred.
Recapture — bringing previously claimed depreciation back into income when depreciable property sells for more than its written-down tax cost.

hostile.q: You want to sell us the shares, but the company carries a large latent gain and recapture. Why should we pay full price for that tax?
hostile.a: You should not, and I am not asking you to. I have calculated the latent tax and its present value given your likely holding period, and my asking price already reflects a share of it. In exchange, you avoid the transfer taxes and costs of an asset transfer, and I will give you full tax indemnities and a clean tax-history file for the company. Let us agree the latent-tax number first, then the price.

role: Failure forensics, with Cole on audit and integrity
title: The Exit Priced as a Share Sale and Taxed as an Asset Sale
summary: This is a composite example. A developer agreed a headline price on the assumption that he would sell shares, then discovered late that the buyer would only buy the building and that his property-rich shares were taxable in the country where the land sat anyway. The deal closed, but most of the expected profit went to tax and price cuts he had never modelled.
body:
This is a composite example. A developer shook hands on a price that only worked as a share sale, and found out after the handshake that the buyer would not buy shares and the tax law would not treat his shares the way he thought.

Recall

Q. What is the exchange spread on a currency conversion?

A. The difference between the bank's buying and selling rates; its margin, which you can negotiate in writing before a large conversion.

Q. What usually goes wrong first when a customs or indirect-tax position fails?

A. Classification or valuation was assumed rather than confirmed, and nobody kept the evidence that the conditions of a relief were met.

Q. Why is a substance record kept?

A. To prove, with evidence made at the time, where decisions were really taken and by whom, so that residence and permanent-establishment positions can be defended years later.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this failure was not a market failure or a construction failure. The building was finished, let and valued exactly as planned. The failure was in the tax and documents around the sale, and it was visible in the paperwork long before closing. That makes it preventable, which is the only kind of failure worth studying. The facts are a composite of patterns that recur at exit; the numbers are hypothetical and the tax rates are assumptions for teaching.

1. Timeline

A developer resident in one country builds a 40-unit apartment building in a second country through a local company he owns through a holding company. In year 5 the building is stabilised and a buyer offers 20,000,000 dollars. The developer's model assumes a share sale: his holding company sells the local company's shares, and he believes, from a conversation years earlier, that a treaty means the gain is not taxed in the country where the building sits. He agrees the headline price in a letter of intent. In week 3 of diligence, the buyer's lawyers state that their lender requires an asset purchase. In week 5, the developer's new tax adviser points out that the relevant treaty allows the source country to tax gains on shares that derive their value mainly from land in that country. In week 8 the deal closes as an asset sale, with company tax and recapture inside the local company, a transfer tax the developer had agreed to bear, and withholding on the distribution out.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Agreeing a headline price in the letter of intent without agreeing the form of sale. Relying on an old, informal view of the treaty instead of a current written opinion. And, at the start, holding the building in a way that left no exit route that was both tax-efficient and acceptable to the likely buyer's lender.

3. Assumptions

The developer assumed that shares are always taxed only where the shareholder lives. Many treaties include a clause that lets the country where the land is located tax gains on property-rich shares [unverified — confirm independently]. He assumed the buyer would accept a share purchase. He assumed the transfer-tax clause in the letter of intent, "seller bears transfer taxes", was cheap, because no transfer tax arises on many share sales. Each assumption was reasonable in isolation. None was tested.

4. Incentives

The broker was paid on the headline price and closing, not on net proceeds, so the headline mattered more to him than the form. The buyer's lender wanted a clean asset with no inherited history, and lost nothing by insisting. The developer wanted the deal done before rates rose and accepted terms quickly. Nobody at the table was paid to protect the developer's after-tax number except an adviser he hired after the price was set.

5. Warning signs ignored

The letter of intent said nothing about the form of sale. The buyer was a fund whose lenders routinely require asset purchases. The treaty view came from a conversation, not a written opinion, and was years old. The tax-history file for the local company did not exist, so nobody could say quickly what the latent gain and recapture were. Cole's point: every one of those signs was in a document, and a single afternoon's review would have found them.

Say that out loud now.

Never agree a price before agreeing the form of sale and who bears the tax it creates.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the signed letter of intent. It fixed the price and made the developer bear transfer taxes, while leaving the form open for the buyer to decide. After that, the developer could renegotiate only by threatening to walk away from a buyer he needed, at a time rates were rising.

A hypothetical reconstruction of the arithmetic, for teaching. The developer's model, as a share sale with no source tax: 20,000,000 dollars less his 12,000,000 dollars of cost and debt payoff leaves 8,000,000 dollars. The actual result, as an asset sale: the local company's taxable gain, including recapture, is 7,000,000 dollars, taxed at an assumed 25 percent, so 1,750,000 dollars. A transfer tax at an assumed 2 percent of price is 400,000 dollars. Distributing the remainder triggers withholding at an assumed 10 percent on about 5,850,000 dollars of profit, roughly 585,000 dollars. Expected profit 8,000,000 dollars; actual profit about 5,265,000 dollars. About a third of the gain disappeared between the letter of intent and closing, with the building unchanged.

7. Root cause

The root cause was designing the exit at the exit. The structure, the treaty position and the form of sale were treated as details to settle after the price, when in truth they decided what the price was worth.

The prevention rule

Rule 64: Never agree a price until I have agreed the form of sale, confirmed the tax of that form in a current written opinion, and fixed in writing who bears every tax the sale creates.

What Cole would have audited

Before the letter of intent, a short audit of four documents would have changed the result. The structure chart, to see that property-rich shares were exposed in the source country. The treaty, read with a current adviser. The company's tax-history file, to price the latent gain and recapture. And the draft letter of intent, to see that form of sale and tax allocation were missing. Total cost: a few days of advisers' time. Hypothetical saving: most of 2,700,000 dollars.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the letter of intent, which feels non-binding, fixes the economic terms while leaving the tax-deciding terms open. The control is a rule that every letter of intent states the form of sale, the allocation of transfer taxes and the treatment of latent tax. Professional sign-off required: a tax adviser in each relevant country, in writing, before the letter is signed.

The beginner's mistake

Treating a remembered tax view as advice. Advice is a written opinion, on current law, on your actual facts, with a stated scope.

Callback

In Week 20, LEX taught that letters of intent and term sheets can bind more than people think, and that the terms left out are as important as the terms written in. In Week 57, Elias taught that treaties allocate taxing rights and that their exceptions matter. This failure is those two lessons meeting at the exit.

Recap

A composite developer agreed a price that worked only as a share sale. The buyer required an asset sale, the treaty let the source country tax property-rich shares, and the developer had agreed to bear transfer taxes. About a third of the expected profit went to tax. Rule 64: agree the form of sale and who bears its tax before agreeing the price.

Next: Sage on The Money: comparing an asset sale and a share sale after tax, and pricing the latent gain.
checklist: Every letter of intent I sign states the form of sale.
Every letter of intent allocates transfer taxes and latent tax in writing.
I hold a current written tax opinion on the exit before agreeing a price.
I check whether a treaty lets the source country tax property-rich shares.
I know whether the likely buyer's lender requires an asset purchase.
I model net proceeds, not the headline price, before negotiating.
I align my broker's incentive with net proceeds where I can.
head: Field checklist
rule: Rule 64: Never agree a price until I have agreed the form of sale, confirmed the tax of that form in a current written opinion, and fixed in writing who bears every tax the sale creates.
speak: This is a composite example. A developer agreed a twenty million dollar headline price in a letter of intent, assuming a share sale that he believed was untaxed in the country where the building sat. Then the buyer's lender required an asset purchase, and his new adviser pointed out that the treaty let that country tax gains on property-rich shares anyway. He had also agreed to bear transfer taxes, which cost little on a share sale and a lot on an asset sale. The deal closed as an asset sale with company tax, recapture, transfer tax and withholding on the way out, and about a third of his expected profit went to tax. The building never changed; the paperwork did. The root cause was designing the exit at the exit. My rule is Rule 64: never agree a price until I have agreed the form of sale, confirmed its tax in a current written opinion and fixed who bears every tax the sale creates.
terms: Letter of intent — a preliminary document recording proposed deal terms, which may bind on some points and not others.
Property-rich shares — shares that derive most of their value from land, which some treaties let the land's country tax on sale.
Latent gain — an untaxed gain inside a company, waiting to be realised when the company sells the asset.

hostile.q: Your letter of intent fixes the price but not the form of sale. What happens to your number if we insist on buying the asset?
hostile.a: My number falls by the company-level tax, recapture and transfer tax an asset sale creates, which I have calculated. So I will not sign this letter as drafted. I am proposing either a share sale with a negotiated adjustment for the latent tax, or an asset sale at a price that covers the extra tax, with transfer taxes shared. We agree the form and the tax allocation first, then the price.

title: Asset or Shares: Comparing the Exits After Tax
summary: The right form of sale is the one that leaves the seller more money after tax and after the buyer's price adjustment. A buyer values the latent tax it inherits at a discount, because it may never pay it or may pay it years later. The negotiation is over how that discount is shared.
body:
The headline price is not the number that matters. The number that matters is what reaches you after the buyer's adjustment for latent tax and after every tax the form of sale creates. Compare the two forms on that number, and only that number.

Recall

Q. What is a capital-control trigger in a currency plan?

A. A named, observable signal, such as new rationing rules or a widening gap between official and market rates, that obliges you to move money or accelerate distributions before the gate narrows.

Q. How does an investment concession change a project's cash flow?

A. It removes or defers a tax or duty, which lowers cost or improves cash flow, but only while its conditions are met. The relief belongs in the pro forma with its conditions and its clawback risk beside it.

Q. What is a permanent establishment?

A. A fixed place of business, or in some cases a dependent agent, through which a foreign enterprise carries on business in a country, giving that country the right under a treaty to tax the business profits attributable to it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, on a stabilised building the choice between an asset sale and a share sale can move the seller's proceeds by a material share of the profit. That is often more than you can gain by negotiating the headline price harder. A developer who can compare the two forms in his head, at the table, negotiates the right thing. All numbers are hypothetical, and the tax rates are assumptions for teaching, not any country's law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The seller's two numbers

In plain English: work out what you keep in each case.

The professional framing is the seller's net proceeds under each form. Use one company holding one building, with a tax cost of 6,000,000 dollars, no debt for simplicity, and a market value of 10,000,000 dollars. Assume a company tax rate of 25 percent on the gain, and a shareholder tax on distributions or on share gains of 15 percent.

Asset sale. The company sells for 10,000,000 dollars. Gain 4,000,000; company tax 1,000,000. The company distributes 9,000,000. The shareholder's taxable amount on distribution, assume, is the 3,000,000 of after-tax profit, taxed at 15 percent, 450,000. Net to shareholder: 8,550,000 dollars.

Share sale at full value. The shareholder sells shares for 10,000,000 dollars with a share cost of 6,000,000. Gain 4,000,000, taxed at 15 percent, 600,000. Net: 9,400,000 dollars. On these assumptions the share sale is worth 850,000 dollars more to the seller.

The buyer's discount for latent tax

In plain English: the buyer of shares takes on the company's old tax cost, so it will want a lower price.

The professional framing is the latent tax discount: the reduction in price a buyer of shares asks for to compensate for the tax that will arise inside the company when it eventually sells the building, because it gets no fresh tax cost. The full latent tax here is 25 percent of 4,000,000, which is 1,000,000 dollars. But the buyer may hold for ten years, or never sell the building directly, so the present value of that tax to the buyer is less than 1,000,000. A buyer also loses the higher depreciation it would have claimed on a fresh tax cost, which has its own value. In practice the discount is negotiated somewhere between a modest fraction and nearly all of the latent tax. That range is commercial practice, not a rule.

A worked example. Suppose the buyer asks for a 600,000 dollar discount. The share price becomes 9,400,000 dollars. Gain 3,400,000, shareholder tax 510,000. Net: 8,890,000 dollars. Still 340,000 dollars better than the asset sale's 8,550,000. Now suppose the buyer asks for the full 1,000,000. Price 9,000,000; gain 3,000,000; tax 450,000; net 8,550,000. Exactly equal to the asset sale. That is the seller's walk-away discount: above it, the asset sale wins.

Say that out loud now.

I compare net to net. The share sale wins only while the buyer's discount is smaller than the tax the share sale saves me.

Adding the transaction taxes and recapture

Two more lines usually tilt the answer. First, transfer taxes on land: in many places an asset sale of land attracts a transfer tax that a share sale may avoid, unless a look-through rule catches the share sale too. Second, recapture: if the company has claimed depreciation, an asset sale brings it back as income, often taxed less favourably than a gain, while a share sale leaves it latent for the buyer to price.

A second worked example. Add a 2 percent transfer tax on an asset sale, 200,000 dollars, borne by the seller, and 1,000,000 dollars of recapture within the 4,000,000 gain taxed, by assumption, at the same company rate, so no change in company tax but a larger latent liability for a share buyer. The asset sale net falls to about 8,370,000 dollars once the transfer tax reduces the distribution. The walk-away discount on the share sale rises accordingly, because the asset route has become more expensive. The general lesson: list every tax each form creates, then find the discount at which the two forms are equal. That breakeven discount is your negotiating limit.

How the best do it

Sophisticated sellers prepare a vendor tax pack before marketing: the tax cost of each asset, depreciation claimed, latent gain, any elections, and a clean tax-history file with clearances where available. It shortens diligence and narrows the buyer's discount, because uncertainty is priced as risk. A small developer can copy this with a five-page pack and a current written opinion attached.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's point for your personal balance sheet: record each property interest at its value net of latent tax, not at market value. A building worth 10,000,000 dollars inside a company with 1,000,000 dollars of latent tax is not a 10,000,000 dollar asset to you; it is roughly 8,500,000 to 9,400,000 depending on how it is eventually sold. Your net worth, your liquidity planning and your estate plan should use the realistic number. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any of it.

Reading the table at the table

Carry the comparison as a two-column table: asset sale on the left, share sale on the right, and one row for each item: price, selling costs, transfer tax, company tax including recapture, debt repaid, shareholder tax or withholding, and net. Below it, one more row: the breakeven discount. When an offer arrives, fill in the price and read the net. When a buyer changes the form, move the price to the other column. The table does not tell you what to accept. It tells you what each offer is worth, which is the only fact you need to negotiate well.

Update the assumptions whenever advice changes. A new written opinion that a look-through rule applies to the share sale moves a number on the right; a revised depreciation schedule moves recapture on the left. The table is only as current as its inputs.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is comparing headline prices instead of net proceeds, so you accept a lower discount on a share sale that is in fact worse than an asset sale once transfer taxes and recapture are counted. The control is a two-column net-proceeds table, updated for every offer.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming the buyer will pay full value for shares because "it is the same building". It is the same building with a different tax history, and the buyer knows it.

Callback

In Week 10, Sage taught that value is net operating income divided by the cap rate. That is the building's value. This lesson adds the layer below it: the value to you is what survives the form of sale. A cap rate tells you what the asset is worth; the net-proceeds table tells you what the exit is worth.

Recap

Compare the forms on net proceeds. A share sale usually saves company-level tax and transfer tax, but the buyer discounts the price for the latent tax it inherits. The breakeven discount, where the two forms leave you the same money, is your negotiating limit. Value your own holdings net of latent tax.

Next: Devika on The Rules: how the law decides what you sold and who taxes it.
checklist: I compare exit forms on net proceeds, never on headline price.
I calculate the latent tax inside each company I own.
I know my breakeven discount for a share sale.
I list transfer taxes and recapture for each form of sale.
I prepare a vendor tax pack before marketing an asset.
I value my personal holdings net of latent tax.
I update the net-proceeds table for every new offer.
head: Field checklist
speak: I compare an asset sale and a share sale on one number: what reaches me after tax. Hypothetically, a company holds a building worth ten million dollars with a tax cost of six million. As an asset sale, the company pays tax on the four million gain, then I pay tax on the distribution, and I net about eight and a half million. As a share sale at full price, I pay tax once on the share gain and net about nine point four million. But the buyer inherits the company's latent tax of about one million and will ask for a discount. If the discount is six hundred thousand, the share sale still wins. If it reaches the full million, the two forms are equal, and that is my walk-away limit. Transfer taxes and recapture move that limit, so I list every tax each form creates, prepare a vendor tax pack before marketing, and value my own holdings net of latent tax.
terms: Net proceeds — what the seller keeps after the price adjustment and every tax the form of sale creates.
Latent tax discount — the price reduction a share buyer asks for to reflect the tax it inherits inside the company.
Vendor tax pack — a seller's prepared file on the tax history and latent tax of the assets being sold.

hostile.q: We will buy your shares, but only at a discount equal to the full latent tax. Why would we take less?
hostile.a: Because you will not pay that tax for years, if ever, and its present value is well below its face amount. You also avoid the transfer tax and costs of an asset transfer, and you get a clean tax file with indemnities. My breakeven is the full latent tax; above it I would rather sell the asset. So let us split the difference between its present value and its face value.

title: How the Law Decides What You Sold and Who Taxes It
summary: At exit, four bodies of rules decide the tax: the rules that characterise the sale, the transaction taxes on land and business transfers, the look-through and clearance rules for non-resident sellers, and the departure tax concepts that apply when the owner, not the building, moves. Each is technical and changes; know the questions, then get written advice.
body:
The law does not care what you call the sale. It looks at what legally changed hands, where the value sits and who the seller is, and taxes accordingly. Four sets of rules decide the answer, and one of them applies even if you never sell anything.

Recall

Q. Name the three rulebooks that govern moving money across a border.

A. Investment screening and registration, exchange and capital-movement rules, and anti-money-laundering law with its beneficial-ownership duties.

Q. What is the difference between a tax that is exempt and one that is zero-rated in a value-added tax system?

A. In many systems, a zero-rated supply is taxable at a rate of zero, so input tax credits can usually still be claimed, while an exempt supply is outside the tax and input credits are usually lost. The labels and effects vary by country.

Q. What is a tie-breaker rule in a tax treaty?

A. A rule that decides which country a person or entity is resident in for treaty purposes when both countries' own laws claim it as resident.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the exit is where tax authorities pay closest attention, because large sums move once and the seller may be leaving the country. Every rule in this lesson exists to stop value leaving untaxed. You will not memorise the detail. You will learn the four questions that tell you which detail to ask your advisers about. Nothing here is a jurisdictional conclusion; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Rule set one: characterising the sale

In plain English: the law first decides what kind of thing you sold.

The professional framing is characterisation. Did the seller sell land, a building, depreciable equipment, goodwill, shares or a partnership interest? Each has different tax rules. In an asset sale, the purchase price must be allocated among the assets, land, building, fixtures, and the allocation matters: land is usually not depreciable, so a buyer wants more price on the building and the seller may want more on the land to reduce recapture. Many systems require buyer and seller to use a consistent allocation, and authorities can challenge one that does not reflect value [unverified — confirm independently]. The habit is to agree the allocation in the sale agreement, supported by a valuation.

Rule set two: transaction taxes

In plain English: some taxes are charged on the transfer itself, whether or not you made a profit.

The professional framing covers land transfer taxes or stamp duties charged on the conveyance of land, and value-added tax or goods and services tax that may apply to sales of new or commercial property. Two points matter at exit. First, a share sale may avoid land transfer tax, but many jurisdictions have rules that treat the transfer of a controlling interest in a land-rich company as a transfer of the land [unverified — confirm independently]. Second, the sale of a whole operating property may qualify for going-concern relief from value-added tax, but only if strict conditions are met, often including that the buyer continues the same activity and is registered [unverified — confirm independently].

A worked example, hypothetical. A building sells for 10,000,000 dollars. Land transfer tax at an assumed 2 percent on an asset sale is 200,000 dollars. In a share sale, if no look-through rule applies, that tax may not arise. If a look-through rule does apply to a transfer of control of a land-rich company, it may arise anyway. That single rule can change which form of sale wins on Day 3's table.

Rule set three: non-resident sellers and clearance

In plain English: if the seller lives elsewhere, the country where the land is wants its tax before the money leaves.

The professional framing is the combination of source taxation of property-rich shares and clearance certificates: many countries tax non-residents on gains from local land, and some extend that to shares deriving their value mainly from local land, as treaties often allow. To enforce it, some require the buyer to withhold part of the price from a non-resident seller unless the seller obtains a clearance certificate from the tax authority, after paying or securing the tax [unverified — confirm independently]. The practical effect is timing: if clearance takes months, a portion of your price sits with the buyer or the authority.

Say that out loud now.

What did I sell, what does the transfer itself cost, and will the land's country hold back my price until I am cleared?

Rule set four: departure tax concepts

In plain English: in some countries, if you stop being resident, the law treats you as if you sold your assets on the day you left.

The professional framing is departure tax, sometimes called a deemed disposition on emigration: when an individual ceases to be resident, certain property is deemed sold at fair market value, and tax is due on the resulting gain even though no sale took place and no cash was received [unverified — confirm independently]. Some countries exclude local land from the deemed sale, because they keep the right to tax it later anyway, and some allow the tax to be deferred if security is posted [unverified — confirm independently]. Shares of a company that holds foreign property, however, can be caught.

A second worked example, hypothetical. An individual holds shares in a holding company, cost 1,000,000 dollars, worth 5,000,000 dollars, and moves to another country. If a departure tax applies to those shares, a 4,000,000 dollar gain is deemed realised. At an assumed 20 percent effective rate, 800,000 dollars of tax falls due with no sale and no cash. The decision that caused it was a move, not a transaction. That is why departure tax belongs in the exit plan of anyone who might change country.

Professional sign-off required: a tax adviser in each relevant country, and in the country of residence before any move.

Putting the four questions to work

Before marketing a building, send each adviser four written questions. One: what will the sale be characterised as in each form, and what allocation of price do you recommend? Two: what transaction taxes arise in each form, and does any look-through rule apply to a share sale? Three: if the seller is non-resident, is withholding or a clearance certificate required, and how long does clearance usually take? Four: if any owner might change residence in the next few years, what does departure tax do to their interest? Ask for the answers in writing, with the date and the version of the law relied on. That letter is the core of your exit tax map, and it turns four vague worries into four checked facts.

Diary the clearance timeline as well. If clearance usually takes months, apply before marketing rather than after signing, so the holdback is short or avoided altogether.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating exit tax as a single rate on a single gain. It is four systems working at once: characterisation, transaction taxes, non-resident withholding and clearance, and departure rules. The control is a one-page exit tax map for each asset and each owner, reviewed by advisers before marketing and before any change of residence.

The beginner's mistake

Leaving the purchase-price allocation to the lawyers at the last minute, then finding that it decides how much recapture the seller pays and how much depreciation the buyer gets, and that the buyer has already set it in their favour.

Callback

In Week 23, Devika and Elias drew the real estate tax map: transfer taxes, value-added tax, gains and recapture. This lesson is that map at the exit, with two additions only an international owner meets: the land's country holding back the price, and the owner's own departure being treated as a sale.

Recap

Four rule sets decide exit tax. Characterisation decides what was sold and how the price is allocated. Transaction taxes may apply regardless of profit, and look-through rules can catch share sales. Non-resident sellers may face withholding until cleared. Departure rules can tax an owner who moves. Map all four before marketing.

Next: Elias on The Numbers: reverse engineering the sale price you need from the cash you want to keep.
checklist: I have a one-page exit tax map for each asset and owner.
I agree the purchase-price allocation in the sale agreement with a valuation.
I know whether transfer tax applies to an asset sale and a share sale.
I know whether a look-through rule treats a share sale as a land sale.
I know whether a non-resident clearance certificate is needed and how long it takes.
I check value-added tax going-concern conditions before relying on them.
I take departure tax advice before any change of residence.
I hold written advice from each relevant country before marketing.
head: Field checklist
speak: At exit, four sets of rules decide the tax. First, characterisation: what did I legally sell, land, building, equipment, goodwill or shares, and how is the price allocated among them, because the allocation decides recapture and the buyer's depreciation. Second, transaction taxes: land transfer tax or value-added tax can apply regardless of profit, and some places treat a transfer of control of a land-rich company as a transfer of the land. Third, non-resident sellers: the country where the land sits may tax property-rich shares, and the buyer may have to withhold part of my price until I obtain a clearance certificate. Fourth, departure tax: in some countries, if I stop being resident, I am treated as having sold certain assets on the day I left, with tax due and no cash received. So I keep a one-page exit tax map for every asset and owner, reviewed by advisers before marketing and before any move.
terms: Purchase-price allocation — dividing an asset sale price among land, building and other assets, which decides tax for both sides.
Clearance certificate — a tax authority's confirmation that a non-resident seller's tax is paid or secured, releasing the buyer from withholding.
Departure tax — tax on a deemed sale of certain property when an individual ceases to be resident.

hostile.q: You are a non-resident seller. Why should we not withhold a portion of the price until you produce a clearance certificate?
hostile.a: You should, if the law requires it, and I will not ask you to take that risk. I have already applied for the certificate, and here is the application and our estimate of the tax. If it has not issued by closing, we agree an escrow of the required amount, released to me on the certificate or to the authority if it is refused, so neither of us is exposed.

title: Reverse Engineering the Price You Need
summary: Start from the cash you want in your hands after every tax and cost, and work backward through withholding, company tax, recapture, transfer tax and selling costs to the sale price that delivers it. Do it for an asset sale and a share sale, and you know exactly what each offer must be.
body:
Most sellers start from a price and hope for a net number. Start instead from the net number you need and work backward to the price. Then every offer can be judged in seconds, in either form of sale.

Recall

Q. What is a share sale?

A. A sale of the shares of the company that owns the property, so the property changes hands without itself being transferred, and the buyer inherits the company's tax history.

Q. In an indirect-tax calculation, why does the order of steps matter?

A. Because some taxes are charged on amounts that include other taxes or costs, so applying them in the wrong order gives the wrong base and the wrong answer.

Q. In a substance calculation, what does a count of board meetings by location show?

A. Where decisions were actually taken, which is evidence for, or against, the residence the structure claims.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an even week, so we reverse engineer. When a buyer names a price, you need to know within a minute whether it meets your target in the form they propose. That speed comes from having worked the calculation backward before the meeting. All numbers are hypothetical and every rate is an assumption for teaching, not any country's law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The target and the assumptions

You want 8,000,000 dollars in the hands of your holding company after all tax and costs. The owning company has a building with a tax cost of 5,500,000 dollars, made up of land at 1,500,000 and a depreciated building at 4,000,000, after 1,000,000 dollars of depreciation claimed. There is a loan of 3,000,000 dollars to repay at sale. Assumptions: company tax 25 percent on all gains including recapture; withholding on distributions to the holding company 10 percent; selling costs 2 percent of price; land transfer tax on an asset sale 2 percent of price, borne by the seller; for a share sale, a tax on the holding company's share gain of 15 percent, and the buyer demands a latent-tax discount equal to half the latent tax.

Working backward: the asset sale

Step 1, undo the withholding. If 8,000,000 must arrive after 10 percent withholding, the distribution must be 8,000,000 divided by 0.9, about 8,889,000 dollars.

Step 2, add back the loan. The company must hold 8,889,000 for distribution after repaying 3,000,000 of debt, so it needs about 11,889,000 dollars of cash after its own tax.

Step 3, undo company tax. Let P be the price. Cash after tax equals P, less selling costs of 0.02P, less transfer tax of 0.02P, less tax of 25 percent on the gain. The gain is P less costs less tax cost: P minus 0.04P minus 5,500,000, which is 0.96P minus 5,500,000. Tax is 0.25 times that, 0.24P minus 1,375,000. So cash after tax is 0.96P minus 0.24P plus 1,375,000, which is 0.72P plus 1,375,000.

Step 4, solve. 0.72P plus 1,375,000 equals 11,889,000, so 0.72P equals 10,514,000, and P is about 14,603,000 dollars. Check: costs and transfer tax 584,000; gain about 8,519,000; tax about 2,130,000; cash about 11,889,000; less debt 3,000,000 leaves 8,889,000; less 10 percent withholding leaves about 8,000,000. The asset-sale price you need is about 14,600,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Undo the withholding, add back the debt, undo the company tax, solve for price, then check forward.

Working backward: the share sale

In a share sale the holding company sells shares, the loan stays in the company and the buyer prices it, and there is no land transfer tax, assuming no look-through rule applies.

Step 1, what the buyer pays. The buyer values the company as the building's value V, less the 3,000,000 loan, less a discount of half the latent tax. The latent tax is 25 percent of V minus 5,500,000, so half is 0.125V minus 687,500. Share price S equals V minus 3,000,000 minus 0.125V plus 687,500, which is 0.875V minus 2,312,500.

Step 2, the seller's tax. Assume the holding company's cost in the shares is 2,500,000 dollars, the equity it invested. Selling costs 2 percent of S. Gain is 0.98S minus 2,500,000, taxed at 15 percent. Net is 0.98S minus 0.15 times that, which is 0.833S plus 375,000.

Step 3, solve for S. 0.833S plus 375,000 equals 8,000,000, so S is about 9,154,000 dollars. Then V: 0.875V equals 9,154,000 plus 2,312,500, about 11,466,500, so V is about 13,105,000 dollars.

So, in a share sale, a building value of about 13,100,000 dollars delivers your 8,000,000, against about 14,600,000 in an asset sale. On these assumptions you need about 1,500,000 dollars less building value if the buyer takes shares at a half discount. That gap is what the form of sale is worth.

Using the two targets in the room

Write the two numbers on one card: asset-sale price 14,600,000; share-sale building value 13,100,000 at half discount. A buyer who offers 13,500,000 for the asset fails your target by over 1,000,000. The same buyer offering shares at a building value of 13,500,000 with a half discount clears it. Now you can negotiate the form, not only the number. And if the discount rises from a half to the full latent tax, rerun step 1: the required building value rises, and you know by how much before you answer.

A second check, hypothetical. If a look-through rule makes the share sale bear the same 2 percent transfer tax on building value, add about 262,000 dollars of cost at 13,105,000, and the required value rises by roughly that amount divided by the seller's after-tax share, to around 13,400,000. Still below the asset route, but the gap narrows. One rule, a quarter of a million dollars.

Why the backward solve is honest

A forward calculation starts from the price a buyer has named, and it invites you to stop as soon as the answer looks good enough. A backward solve starts from what you actually need, so the result is a hard floor, not an impression. It also exposes every assumption in a single chain: change the withholding rate, the discount or the debt, and you can see exactly which step moves and by how much. That transparency is what lets you share the structure of the calculation with a partner or lender without revealing the floor itself.

One more discipline. Always state the assumptions above the result, in the same order as the steps: withholding rate, debt, company tax rate, selling costs, transfer tax, share-gain tax and discount. A result without its assumptions is a number nobody can check, and a number nobody can check is not one an investor or lender should rely on.

Finally, run a sensitivity on the one input you trust least. If the latent-tax discount is the softest number, solve again at a third and at the full latent tax and write all three answers on the card. In the room, that range is worth more than a single precise figure.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is solving forward from a headline price and stopping when the answer looks acceptable, without checking the other form or the assumptions. The control is to solve backward for both forms before marketing, and to rerun the solve whenever a rate, a discount or a rule changes.

The beginner's mistake

Forgetting that the loan is repaid out of an asset sale but stays inside the company in a share sale, so the two prices are not comparable until debt is put on the same footing.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage reverse engineered a deal from public information: implied land price, rent and return. Today is the same technique pointed at your own exit. In both cases, fixing the outcome and solving for the input is faster and more honest than guessing an input and hoping for the outcome.

Recap

Fix the net cash you need. For an asset sale, undo withholding, add back debt, undo company tax and solve for price. For a share sale, model the buyer's price after debt and latent-tax discount, then solve. The gap between the two answers is what the form of sale is worth.

Next: JAX on The Room: negotiating the form of sale with a buyer who wants the asset.
checklist: I fix my required net cash before any price discussion.
I solve backward for the asset-sale price, step by step.
I solve backward for the share-sale building value at a stated discount.
I put debt on the same footing before comparing the two forms.
I check each backward solve forward.
I rerun the solve whenever a rate, discount or rule changes.
I carry both target numbers into the negotiation on one card.
head: Field checklist
speak: I reverse engineer my exit from the cash I need. Hypothetically, I want eight million dollars in my holding company after all tax. For an asset sale, I undo the 10 percent withholding, which means distributing about 8.89 million; I add back the three million loan; and I undo company tax, selling costs and transfer tax, which gives a required price of about 14.6 million. For a share sale, the buyer pays building value less the loan less half the latent tax; I undo my 15 percent share-gain tax and selling costs, and find I need a building value of only about 13.1 million. So the form of sale is worth about 1.5 million dollars of building value on these assumptions. I carry both numbers on one card, check every solve forward, and rerun it whenever a rate, a discount or a look-through rule changes.
terms: Required net cash — the after-tax amount a seller must receive, used as the starting point of a backward solve.
Gross-up — dividing a net amount by one minus a tax rate to find the gross amount that delivers it.
Building value — the value of the property itself, before deducting company debt or tax adjustments.

hostile.q: We are offering 13,500,000 for the asset. Why are you saying that does not work for you?
hostile.a: Because after company tax, transfer tax, debt repayment and withholding, an asset sale at 13,500,000 leaves me more than 1,000,000 below my required net. As a share purchase at the same building value, with an agreed discount for latent tax, it works for both of us: you avoid the transfer tax and I clear my number. I can show you both calculations line by line.

title: Negotiating the Form of Sale
summary: A composite scene: a buyer's fund wants to buy your stabilised building as an asset; you want to sell the shares. Learn to put the form of sale on the table before the price, trade the latent tax openly, and keep your walk-away number to yourself.
body:
In an exit negotiation, the form of sale is worth as much as a round of price haggling, and it is negotiated first. Put it on the table early, trade the latent tax in numbers, and let the buyer see you know both calculations.

Recall

Q. In a bank onboarding meeting, what is the question behind "why does this holding company exist?"

A. Whether the entity is there to hide someone or something. You answer that directly, with its registers, owners and purpose.

Q. In a meeting on an indirect-tax concession, what should you never promise?

A. Compliance with conditions you have not checked you can meet, or a timetable you do not control.

Q. In a substance discussion, why must board members actually deliberate?

A. Because a board that only signs what was decided elsewhere puts real management, and possibly residence, where the decisions were really made.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, sellers lose exit value in rooms like this one by negotiating the price first, agreeing a number, and then discovering the form. A price without a form is not a price. This scene teaches you to reverse the order without making the buyer feel ambushed.

The setup

This is a composite scene with hypothetical numbers and assumed tax effects. Your company owns a stabilised building. Your Day 5 card says: as an asset sale you need about 14,600,000 dollars; as a share sale you need a building value of about 13,100,000 at a discount of half the latent tax. The latent tax is about 1,900,000 dollars. Across the table: Hana, acquisitions director of a fund, and Paul, the fund's tax counsel. Hana opened by email at 13,800,000 dollars "for the property".

The opening: form before price

Say: "Thank you for the offer. Before we talk about the number, I want to agree what we are buying and selling, because the form changes what the number is worth to both of us. My preference is to sell you the shares of the property company, with a clean tax file and full indemnities. I understand you may prefer the asset. Can we spend twenty minutes on that first?"

This does three things. It signals that you know the tax, it frames the form as a shared problem, and it stops you from anchoring on 13,800,000 as if it were comparable across forms.

Say that out loud now.

The question behind the question

Paul asks: "Why should we take on your company's history?" The question behind it is: "What hidden liabilities come with these shares, and how will you protect us?" Answer that. Say: "The company has owned one building since it was formed. Here is its tax-history file, its tax filings, and a list of every contract it is party to. We will give tax and general indemnities for the pre-closing period, backed by an escrow for an agreed period." Paul is not really objecting to shares. He is asking what makes them safe.

Hana asks: "What discount for the latent tax are you offering?" The question behind it is: "Do you know the number, and will you be reasonable?" Show the number, not your limit. Say: "The latent tax, at face value, is about 1,900,000 dollars. You will not pay it for years, if ever, so its present value to you is lower. We think a fair discount is between a third and a half of face value."

The lines never to say

Never say "We need at least 8,000,000 net." Your required net and your breakeven discount are your walk-away; once said, they become the buyer's target. Never say "The share sale is better for us on tax"; say instead that it is better for both parties, and show the transfer tax and costs it saves the buyer. Never say "Our advisers say the treaty means no tax here" unless you hold a current written opinion, and even then, do not lead with it; let the buyer's counsel reach their own view. And never accept a price "subject to agreeing structure later". That is Rule 64 broken in one sentence.

When to stay silent

After you name the discount range, stop. Let Paul calculate. Lawyers and analysts often argue themselves toward the middle of a reasoned range if you give them room. If Hana counters with "the full latent tax", do not answer immediately. Look at your card, which says your breakeven is the full latent tax on the share route, and recognise that her counter would leave you exactly indifferent. Then say: "At the full discount there is no reason for us to sell shares. Then we would sell the asset, at a price that covers the extra tax. Shall we price that instead?"

Holding your state

Exit meetings carry years of work, and that weight makes people concede to end the tension. Name the feeling to yourself before the meeting, and decide in advance that you will take a break, out of the room, before agreeing any final number. A short walk is a practitioner habit for resetting, not a proven method, but a pause never cost a seller money and a rushed yes often does.

The close

Say: "So we are agreed in principle on a share purchase, a discount at forty percent of the latent tax, indemnities backed by an escrow, and a price we will now work out on that basis. I will send a revised letter of intent tonight that states the form, the tax allocation and the discount, before the price." Then send it, and do not sign anything that states a price without those three terms beside it.

Founder health

Exit negotiations often run late and run long, and on a rotating shift schedule they collide with sleep. Schedule decisive meetings for the part of your rotation when you are most rested, not the morning after a night shift, and never sign a final document while sleep-deprived. These are general habits; for anything about your own sleep or health, check with your doctor.

If the buyer will not move

Sometimes a buyer's lender genuinely cannot finance a share purchase. Then do not fight the form; price it. Return to your Day 5 card and quote the asset-sale price that meets your net, and offer to share the transfer tax or bear part of it in exchange for that price. Say: "I understand your lender needs the asset. Then the price that works for us is higher, because the asset route creates company tax and transfer tax that a share sale avoids. Here is the difference, line by line." A buyer who sees the arithmetic usually accepts that the form has a price. A buyer who does not was going to discount you on something else anyway.

And if the buyer insists on the asset at a share-sale price, that is the moment to use the break you planned. The answer is usually no, and it is easier to say it rested.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is revealing your breakeven discount or required net, so the buyer prices to it. The control is to share the calculation's structure and the latent tax at face value, never your limit.

The beginner's mistake

Arguing tax law with the buyer's tax counsel. You are not there to win the law; you are there to agree who bears it. Leave the law to the advisers' written exchange.

Callback

In Week 3, Kema taught anchoring: the first number spoken pulls the rest of the negotiation toward it. Here the anchor is subtle. The buyer's 13,800,000 for the asset is not comparable to a share price, so letting it anchor a share negotiation costs you money twice. Reframe the form first, then the number.

Recap

Put the form of sale on the table before the price. Answer the question behind tax counsel's objection with a clean file and indemnities. Name the latent tax and a fair discount range, never your limit. Stay silent after you name it. Close with a revised letter of intent stating form, tax allocation and discount.

Next: Kema on the week's review, with Cole's Auditor's Chair.
checklist: I agree the form of sale before any price.
I bring a clean tax-history file and an indemnity proposal.
I state the latent tax at face value and a fair discount range.
I never reveal my required net or breakeven discount.
I never accept a price subject to agreeing structure later.
I take a break before agreeing any final number.
I schedule decisive meetings when I am most rested.
head: Field checklist
speak: In an exit negotiation I agree the form of sale before the price, because a price without a form is not a price. I open by saying I would like to sell the shares with a clean tax file and indemnities, and ask to settle the form first. When tax counsel asks why they should inherit the company's history, the real question is how I will protect them, so I show the file and offer indemnities backed by escrow. When asked for a discount, I name the latent tax at face value and a fair range, say a third to a half, then stay silent while they calculate. I never reveal my required net or my breakeven discount, never argue tax law with their counsel, and never accept a price subject to agreeing structure later. If they demand the full latent tax, I switch to pricing an asset sale that covers the extra tax. I close with a revised letter of intent stating form, tax allocation and discount.
terms: Walk-away — the least favourable terms a negotiator will accept, kept private.
Indemnity — a promise to compensate the other party for defined losses, such as pre-closing tax.
Escrow — money held by a neutral party and released when agreed conditions are met.

hostile.q: Your letter of intent wants the form and tax allocation agreed before price. Isn't that just a way to delay?
hostile.a: No. It is how we avoid agreeing a number that means two different things. If we agree shares at a stated discount, the price discussion takes an afternoon. If we agree a price first and then discover we meant different forms, we lose weeks renegotiating. I will send the revised letter tonight, and I can be ready to agree price this week.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 64 Review: Asset or Shares, Recapture and Departure
summary: Six questions test the week: the two forms of sale, the latent tax discount, recapture, Rule 64, departure tax and the backward solve. Cole's Auditor's Chair reads a hypothetical exit memo as a hostile auditor would, and the boardroom drill explains the exit in two minutes.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: the exit is taxed the way you built the entry, so you choose the form of sale, and who bears its tax, before you ever agree a price.

Recall

Q. What is the breakeven discount on a share sale?

A. The latent-tax discount at which a share sale leaves the seller exactly the same net proceeds as an asset sale. Above it, the asset sale wins.

Q. In an indirect-tax review, what does a hostile reader look for first?

A. Whether the conditions of every relief claimed were actually met and evidenced at the time, rather than assumed.

Q. What is a substance record?

A. Evidence made at the time of where decisions were taken and by whom, used to defend residence and permanent-establishment positions.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six without notes, you can sit across from a buyer's tax counsel and know which conversation you are in. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What is the difference between an asset sale and a share sale?

Answer: In an asset sale the owning company sells the property, realising the gain and any recapture at company level, and the buyer gets a fresh tax cost. In a share sale the shareholders sell the company, the property keeps its old tax cost, and the buyer inherits the company's history and latent tax.

Question 2. Why does a buyer of shares ask for a latent tax discount?

Answer: Because it inherits the company's low tax cost in the building, so tax on the eventual sale stays inside the company, and it loses the higher depreciation a fresh tax cost would give. It values that at less than face, because the tax may be years away.

Question 3. What is recapture?

Answer: Bringing previously claimed depreciation back into income when depreciable property is sold for more than its written-down tax cost, often taxed less favourably than a capital gain.

Question 4. What was the root cause in the composite exit case, and what is Rule 64?

Answer: Designing the exit at the exit: the price was agreed before the form of sale and its tax were settled. Rule 64: never agree a price until I have agreed the form of sale, confirmed its tax in a current written opinion and fixed in writing who bears every tax the sale creates.

Question 5. What is a departure tax?

Answer: In some countries, a deemed sale of certain property at fair market value when an individual stops being resident, so tax can fall due with no sale and no cash. It must be checked before any move.

Question 6. How do you reverse engineer the price you need from an asset sale?

Answer: Start from the net cash you need. Gross it up for withholding, add back debt repaid at sale, then undo company tax, selling costs and transfer tax to solve for price, and check the answer forward.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Elias and Omar set the frame: an asset sale sells the building, a share sale sells the box, and the choice is made at entry. Ford and Cole took a composite exit priced as a share sale and taxed as an asset sale, giving Rule 64. Sage compared the forms on net proceeds and found the breakeven discount. Devika laid out the four rule sets: characterisation, transaction taxes, non-resident clearance and departure tax. Elias reverse engineered the price needed in each form. JAX negotiated the form before the price.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 64 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: read this hypothetical exit memo as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Exit memo to the board. Recommend accepting the buyer's 15,000,000 dollar offer, form of sale to be agreed in documentation. Tax: our gain is about 6,000,000 dollars and, as we are non-resident, no tax arises in the property's country under the treaty, per advice received at acquisition. Depreciation claimed: not known, as no tax-history file is kept, but immaterial. Transfer taxes: buyer's responsibility, as usual. Net to shareholders: about 12,000,000 dollars after repaying the 3,000,000 dollar loan. Our chairman intends to move abroad next year; no tax implications are expected.

The defects. First, the form of sale is left open while the price is accepted: Rule 64 broken. Second, the treaty view is years old, its scope unknown, and many treaties let the source country tax property-rich shares or land directly; an auditor asks for the written opinion and its date. Third, depreciation claimed is unknown, so recapture cannot be called immaterial; without a tax-history file no one can price the latent tax or the buyer's discount. Fourth, "transfer taxes are the buyer's responsibility, as usual" is an assertion, not a contract term; who pays depends on the agreement and the law. Fifth, the net figure ignores company tax, recapture, transfer tax, selling costs, withholding on distribution and any non-resident clearance holdback, so 12,000,000 is a headline, not a net. Sixth, the chairman's move may trigger departure tax on his shares; "no implications expected" is a guess on a decision that can create tax with no cash.

Then the auditor asks for the evidence that would cure each defect: a draft letter of intent stating form and tax allocation; a current written tax opinion from each country; the company's depreciation schedule and tax cost; the transfer-tax clause and the applicable rule; a net-proceeds calculation for both forms; and departure-tax advice for the chairman, dated before the move. A board that approves a sale without those documents is approving a hope.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "We have an offer; why can't we just say yes?" Then compare.

Model answer: "Because the offer is a headline, and we have not agreed what it buys. If they buy the building, our company pays tax on the gain, including recapture of the depreciation we claimed, possibly a transfer tax, and we pay withholding when the cash comes out. If they buy the company's shares, we may save company tax and transfer tax, but they inherit our latent tax and will cut the price for it. I have worked out the price we need in each form and the discount at which the two are equal. So before we answer, we agree the form, who pays each tax, and the discount, in a revised letter of intent. And because the chairman plans to move, we take departure-tax advice now. Then we answer the number, knowing what it is worth."

Score yourself. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you explain both forms in plain English? Did you name the latent-tax discount and the breakeven? Did you mention departure tax? Inside two minutes? Record again tomorrow if not.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is approving a sale on a headline price while the tax-deciding terms are still open. The control is a board rule: no exit is approved without a net-proceeds calculation for both forms and a current written opinion.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking exit tax is a problem for the accountants after closing. By closing, the decisions that set it have all been made.

Callback

In Week 56, Elias and Ford taught residence and substance. Departure tax is that idea from the other side: residence decides who taxes you while you stay, and leaving can itself be taxed.

Recap

Asset sale or share sale, compared on net proceeds; the buyer's latent tax discount; recapture; four rule sets; departure tax; and the backward solve. Rule 64: agree the form of sale and who bears its tax before agreeing a price.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was about the exit. An asset sale sells the building: the company pays tax on the gain, including recapture of past depreciation, perhaps transfer tax, and shareholders face withholding when cash comes out, while the buyer gets a fresh tax cost. A share sale sells the company: it can save company tax and transfer tax, but the buyer inherits the latent tax and discounts the price for it, and the breakeven discount is my walk-away. Four rule sets decide the tax: what was sold and how the price is allocated, transaction taxes and look-through rules, non-resident withholding and clearance, and departure tax if an owner stops being resident. I reverse engineer the price I need in each form from the net cash I want. And Rule 64: never agree a price until I have agreed the form of sale, confirmed its tax in a current written opinion and fixed who bears every tax it creates.
terms: Tax-history file — the record of an asset's tax cost, depreciation claimed and elections, kept from acquisition.
Breakeven discount — the latent-tax discount at which share and asset sales leave the seller equal net proceeds.
Deemed disposition — a sale treated as happening for tax purposes when no actual sale occurred.

hostile.q: Your board approved this sale. Show me the net-proceeds calculation and the tax opinion it relied on.
hostile.a: Here is the board pack. It contains the net-proceeds table for both an asset and a share sale, the breakeven discount, a current written opinion from counsel in each country dated before approval, the depreciation schedule for recapture, and the revised letter of intent stating form and tax allocation. The board minute records that approval was conditional on those documents.
